problem.h: Drawing panels by hand takes forever
p: Children who love comics usually spend half their time ruling wonky boxes and the other half running out of paper. The story gets lost before it’s finished.
Loose sheets go missing, and a brilliant comic ends up in the recycling.

approach.h: The panels are ready. They just bring the story.
p: Every comic in this book has its own cover page and seven pages of ready-drawn panels in different layouts. There’s an idea at the bottom of each cover in case they’re stuck.
When they’ve finished, it’s a real book of twelve comics, with their name on every one.

faq: Roughly six to twelve. Younger children can draw the pictures and dictate the words, and older ones will enjoy planning proper stories.
Pencil first, then pens or colouring pencils. The pages are white so colours look bright. Heavy markers may show through.
Do they need to be good at drawing?
No. The book itself says stick figures are absolutely fine. Clear is better than perfect.
How is it different from The Storymaker’s Journal?
This one is all comics, on big A4 pages. The Journal is smaller and covers characters, worlds and story ideas, with a little comic making.
Is it good for two children to share?
With twelve comics there’s room to take turns, but most children like having their own book with their name on the certificate.

close.p: All they need is a pencil and a hero.
